subject: psych
title: The bystander effect: a mechanism, then a parable
dek: What diffusion of responsibility claims — then Kitty Genovese, the Times story that launched the teaching example, and the later proof that the parable was not the night.

thumb.alt: Kew Gardens Long Island Rail Road platforms seen from a nearby bridge, 2020.

hero.alt: Train at the Kew Gardens LIRR platforms, photographed from the 82nd Avenue bridge in 2020.
hero.caption: Kew Gardens station, Queens, June 2020 — the railroad cut she parked beside in 1964. This is the place later. It is not a crime-scene photograph. The 1964 press pictures of the night are still under copyright; this capsule does not use them.

honesty: This capsule starts with the concept, not the crime. Catherine “Kitty” Genovese was murdered in Kew Gardens in the early hours of 13 March 1964. The text does not describe wounds or sexual violence. It does not use a police portrait of her or of the killer. The Times story of 27 March 1964 is a primary source that later reporting — including the Times itself in 2016 — found flawed. The psychology that followed is real experimental work. The 38 silent witnesses are not.

glossary.explain: The finding, from laboratory and field studies after 1964, that people are often less likely to help when others are present. Darley and Latané (1968) are the usual first citation. The effect does not require the Times’s 38 witnesses to be true.

Darley and Latané’s term: in a group, each person feels less personally responsible for acting. The more people who could help, the easier it is to assume someone else will. A mechanism tested in labs. Not a transcript of Austin Street.
A second mechanism in the helping literature: each person looks at the others, sees no one moving, and concludes the event is not an emergency. Silence reads as information.

Born 7 July 1935 in Brooklyn; killed 13 March 1964 in Kew Gardens, Queens, at 28. She managed Ev’s Eleventh Hour, a bar in Hollis, and lived on Austin Street with Mary Ann Zielonko. The person is older than the parable.
A residential neighborhood in central Queens, around the Long Island Rail Road station and Austin Street. The murder is a Queens story that the Times turned into a story about the city.
The Kew Gardens street of the apartment and the first attack. Geography, not a stage set.
The number the 27 March 1964 Times story made famous. The headline said 37; the body said 38. Manning, Levine, and Collins (2007) found no evidence that 38 people witnessed the murder.

fun_fact.title: Thirty-seven, or thirty-eight
fun_fact.text: The Times headline of 27 March 1964 counted 37. The story under it counted 38. Reprints have used both. The slip is small and perfect: the number that organized a research program was already unstable on the morning it was printed. What was stable was the moral — a city that would not pick up the phone.

blocks.text: The bystander effect is a claim about groups, not about one Queens street. In its ordinary textbook form it says: a person is less likely to help in an emergency when other people are present. The more potential helpers, the less help. The name that stuck to the mechanism is diffusion of responsibility. Each person feels less personally on the hook. Someone else will call. Someone else is closer. Someone else already knows what this is.

That is a statement about psychology. It can be true, false, or true only sometimes. It does not, by itself, require a famous murder, a number of windows, or a city that had forgotten how to be a neighbor. Those arrived later, as a story to hang the claim on.

A second, related claim in the same literature is pluralistic ignorance: people treat other people’s inaction as information. If no one moves, the smoke is not a fire. If no one calls, the noise is not a crime. Silence becomes evidence. Diffusion of responsibility is about who must act. Pluralistic ignorance is about whether anything is happening. Textbooks often braid them. They are not the same sentence.

sections.title: Why psychologists thought a group could freeze a person

blocks.text: John Darley and Bibb Latané designed emergencies you could run twice. A subject hears a seizure over an intercom, or sees smoke under a door, alone or with other people present — sometimes other subjects, sometimes confederates who have been told not to move. In 1968, in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, they reported “Bystander Intervention in Emergencies: Diffusion of Responsibility”: group size inhibited intervention. The 1970 book is The Unresponsive Bystander. The Genovese name is in the preface of a field. The data are from rooms where the experimenters could count.

Why did they think it worked that way? Because responsibility, in their account, is not a fixed moral stock. It divides. A person alone owns the next move. A person in a group can wait, look, and assume the waiting is shared. Add the fear of doing the wrong thing in public — of being the one who overreacts — and inaction has two supports: I am not the one, and this may not be the thing. That is the theory. It is a theory about laboratories and, later, field studies. It is not yet a theory about Austin Street.

sections.title: Kew Gardens, the Times, and the correction

blocks.text: The teaching example came from a newspaper. Kew Gardens in 1964 was a Queens neighborhood of brick apartments, a Long Island Rail Road station, and Austin Street shops. Catherine Genovese, 28, managed Ev’s Eleventh Hour, a bar in Hollis, and shared an apartment at 82–70 Austin Street with Mary Ann Zielonko. There was no 911. A neighbor who wanted the police dialed a precinct or the operator. The city around them had other headlines: a World’s Fair opening in Flushing Meadows; a Civil Rights Act moving through Congress; a press already fond of the phrase urban apathy.

blocks.alt: Wide panoramic photograph of Kew Gardens, Long Island, looking west to east, about 1936.
blocks.caption: Kew Gardens, west to east, about 1936 — Irving Underhill, Library of Congress. A generation before 1964 the neighborhood was already a grid around the railroad. The crime did not invent the place. The parable later made the place a stage.
blocks.credit: Irving Underhill / Library of Congress / no known restrictions

blocks.text: In the early morning of 13 March 1964 Winston Moseley attacked Genovese on the Austin Street side of the building. A neighbor, Robert Mozer, shouted; Moseley left and came back. The second attack was in a rear hallway, out of the street’s sight. Later reconstructions — Kevin Cook, the Times in 2016, the 2007 American Psychologist paper — agree on the shape: two attacks, not three; a layout that made a single continuous audience impossible. She was taken away by ambulance and died on the way to the hospital. Sophia Farrar, a neighbor, had gone to her and held her until help came.

blocks.alt: Kew Gardens LIRR station and the parking lot south of the tracks, seen from Lefferts Boulevard in 2019.
blocks.caption: The station and the south parking lot from Lefferts Boulevard, 3 May 2019. Genovese parked in the railroad lot, about a hundred feet from the apartment door. The cars and the signage are of this century. The cut in the ground is the same fact.

blocks.text: The Times of 14 March ran a short notice. The story that lasted was assigned two weeks later, after Police Commissioner Michael J. Murphy told metropolitan editor A. M. Rosenthal, over lunch, that the Queens case was “one for the books.” Martin Gansberg’s piece of 27 March 1964 went on page one: “37 Who Saw Murder Didn’t Call the Police.” The text said thirty-eight. It said they had watched. It said none had called. An unidentified neighbor supplied the line the decade needed: “I didn’t want to get involved.” Rosenthal’s book the same year was Thirty-Eight Witnesses.

blocks.alt: A paved alley and stair from the Kew Gardens LIRR station toward Lefferts Boulevard, photographed in 2019, empty of people.
blocks.caption: The alley between the station and Lefferts Boulevard, 3 May 2019 — the ground the case is attached to, in daylight, without a body. It is here as geography, not as evidence of what any window saw.

blocks.text: Social psychology moved faster than the corrections. Darley and Latané started from the story the papers had already told. Many textbooks gave the experiments those 38 windows anyway. In 2007, in “The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping,” Rachel Manning, Mark Levine, and Alan Collins went back to the archive and wrote that there was “no evidence for the presence of 38 witnesses, or that witnesses observed the murder, or that witnesses remained inactive.” The Times, in Robert D. McFadden’s 2016 obituary of Moseley, called the 1964 account flawed and “grossly exaggerated.” Jim Rasenberger’s “Kitty, 40 Years Later” (2004) had already begun the paper’s own reconsideration. An editor’s note was later appended to the online 1964 story.

sections.title: What the case still teaches — and what it taught wrongly

blocks.text: What it taught wrongly is easy to list. There were not 38 people at 38 windows watching a single continuous crime and choosing, each of them, not to dial. Some neighbors did call. Someone went downstairs. The layout and the two attacks made a theater audience impossible. Frances Cherry and others later argued that a woman’s voice at 3 a.m. was often filed as a private quarrel — a gendered reading the urban-apathy parable did not pause for. James Solomon’s film The Witness records reporters who already doubted Gansberg’s count and did not pick the fight with Rosenthal. The number that organized a research program was already unstable on the morning it was printed: the headline said 37, the story said 38.

What the case still teaches is not a shrug. Some neighbors did too little. The emergency number was a maze. A press story can fit a ready moral — urban apathy, a city of strangers — and become harder to unwrite than to run. The bystander literature is larger than one street and has been tested without Gansberg’s count. The teaching problem is the one this capsule is for: a discipline can be right about a mechanism and still be wrong about the story it uses to make students care.

Keep the experiments. Label the parable. Do not let the correction become a second simplification — that no one failed anyone that night, or that groups never freeze a person. Diffusion of responsibility does not need 38 silent windows. It never did.
If a field’s most famous example turns out to be a parable, what should it do with the example — drop it, label it, or keep using it because the experiment still works?
